div.head: This paper presents a performance comparison of real-time s y s t e m architectures. A discrete eventdriven, task-based simulator is developed f o r evaluating the performance of parallel and distributed realt i m e systems. Real-time s y s t e m components such as processor, network architectures, and scheduling poZicy are included in the simulator. Simulation results show that priority-based communication and scheduling are more suitable f o r real-time systems t h a n FIFO-based.
div.p: T h e strategy of having a dedicated processor, which produces n o effect o n task ezecution by scheduling and packet/interrupt handling, is proven t o enhance schedulability and predictability. This paper suggests a method f o r finding a n appropriate real-time architecture f o r users having real-time requirements through the performance prediction of real-time systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In applying computer systems to various fields, realtime operations are demanded in innumerable critical areas such as process control, manufacturing, and aircraft control. In such real-time applications, we should be able to guarantee that operations complete before task-completion deadlines since missing the timing requirements could produce a catastrophic result. However, it is impossible to guarantee the real-time readiness o f a system if the system is designed without cont This work was initiated from the Winter Institute Program supported by the Japan-Korea Industrial Technology Cooperation Foundation (JKF).

It is very important to find proper real-time system architectures for users having real-time requirements. However, until now, few works have addressed the problem of finding proper real-time system architectures for the given environments. In this paper, we discuss for finding proper architectures given real-time requirements.

Simulation is used to compare various design alternatives. A simulator can produce the sequences of events expected in the real system and enable us to repeat experiments easily in many different environments. We developed a real-time simulator for dynamic, complex, parallel and distributed real-time systems. The simulator is a discrete event-driven, task-based simulator that enables us to predict the run-time behavior of a specified real-time architecture given a user's execution environment. Also, the simulator is designed to incorporate many design alternatives easily. Using this simulator, we can evaluate the performance of various real-time architectures and find the most suitable architecture for the given environment.

This paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we present the real-time system model that is the basis for developing the simulator. Section 3 explains restrictions and assumptions used in the simulation. Section 4 shows the performance of real-time architectures in various real-time execution environments and discusses how to find a proper architecture in real-time applications using the simulator. In section 5, we summarize and conclude the paper.

div.head: Characteristics of Real-Time Systems
div.p: The real-time system model used in this paper is a parallel and distributed real-time system in which multiple processing nodes are connected by an interconnection network. There is no centralized scheduler. Tasks arrive in each node and can be executed on any node. The only requirement of a task is to guarantee task completion before its deadline.

One of the most important aspects of a real-time system is predictability of system behavior, including a predictable interconnection network. Predictability of network performance depends on the interconnection network and routing/arbitration algorithms used. For instance, in an n x n omega network with a priority forwarding scheme, the worst-case communication delay for the highest priority packet is known to be O(log2 n) [l]. We assume a network model whose worst-case communication delay is predictable.

A real-time task is commonly characterized by three parameters, i.e., its start time, worst-case execution time, and deadline [2]. When a new task arrives at a node in a parallel/distributed system, it must be decided whether the task is guaranteed to be executed on the node in which it arrived or permitted to be sent to another node. It is also decided which task among the guaranteed tasks in the node will be executed first. This process is assumed and is referred to as scheduZing in this paper.

Usually, a real-time task has a priority level depending on how quickly a task must respond. A realtime system can be designed to allow a user to specify the priority of a task according to the urgency of the task. Otherwise, a system may give priority to a real-time task based on the scheduling policy. The scheduler decides the priority of a task based on arrival rate, execution time, and deadline of the task. If the scheduling policy is rate-monotonic for a system which comprises mainly periodic tasks, tasks that execute at a higher rate are assigned a higher priority than tasks that execute at a lower rate. In a system with mainly aperiodic tasks, earliest-deadline-first scheduling or least-laxity-first scheduling are commonly used. Earliest-deadline-first scheduling uses the deadline of a task for giving priority and least-laxity-first scheduling uses laxity which is such as deadline minus execution time. In real-time systems, scheduling is the most important aspect in improving the performance. Many researchers are trying to find efficient scheduling methods in various real-time systems.

div.head: Scheduling Overhead
div.p: A task invokes various extra operations in addition to the execution of the task itself. Examples of these operations are checking the guarantee of a newly arrived task, task startup/termination, and task switching if preemptive scheduling is allowed. We denote these operations as scheduling overhead, which requires extra execution time.
In real-time systems, scheduling overhead makes scheduling difficult due to its lack of predictability.

Usually, a scheduler is invoked frequently but requires a small amount of time (the scheduler should be executed and decide quickly) for operation. However, even though scheduling takes a small amount of time when it is invoked, sometimes it causes a problem in real-time systems.

Consider the situation when a node is very busy executing a current urgent task and has no spare time to schedule for future newly arrived tasks. When a new task arrives, there are a number of ways of handling it. One approach is interrupting the currently running task and scheduling the new task. This approach makes the currently running task miss its deadline. Another approach is to just wait until the node has spare time to schedule the new task. Such a system causes the new task to miss its deadline, even though there may be other nodes in which the task could be executed to meet its deadline.

As a solution for this unpredictable scheduling overhead problem, Stankovic [3] suggested a method in which scheduling is executed as a periodic task. These scheduling tasks consist of a local scheduler and a bidder task. Periodic scheduling enables checking of a new task without much delay. However, this periodic operation invokes overhead due to frequent preemp tion of the currently running task and needless operations during periods when new tasks or new bidder messages do not arrive. Such reserved time for scheduling also results in decreased schedulability for general real-time tasks.

It is possible to have a more flexible management method that keeps the balance of the loads among nodes (sometimes a load is represented as CPU utilization). In this method, surplus time is usually available for the scheduler until the overall system is overloaded. This method enhances schedulability and is accepted as one reasonable solution for that problem. For example, the scheduler keeps new tasks in the arrived node until the utilization of the node reaches some predefined threshold value (e.g., 50%). When the utilization reaches this predefined value, the scheduler starts to send newly arrived tasks to other nodes even though the node can execute the task to meet its deadline. The node is processed by the scheduler as long as already guaranteed tasks meet their deadlines after being processed by the scheduler.

One good hardware solution is suggested in CODA [4, 51. A dedicated processor for each node is provided to handle overhead operations such as scheduling and interrupt handling. The CODA pro- cessor consists of two pipelines. One is the IP (instruction pipeline) for execution of the highest priority task. The other is the PP (packet pipeline) for packet handling, interrupt handling, and scheduling (which includes the local scheduling task and bidder task for global scheduling). PP can be also used for executing second-highest-priority tasks or non-real-time tasks. In PP, scheduling, packet handling, and interrupt handling can have higher priority than execution of general tasks. Such a dedicated processor satisfies the predictability of real-time systems and makes scheduling easy.

div.head: Functional Structure of Real-Time System Model
div.p: The real-time system model used in this paper is a generalisation of parallel and distributed real-time systems. The node structure of our real-time system can be modeled functionally as shown in Fig. 1.

Real-time tasks are generated in each node by the task generator with arrival time, execution time, and deadline. The priority of a task is decided by the scheduler depending on the scheduling policy.

Scheduling is done by a local scheduler and a global scheduler, whose scheduling activities are partially adapted from [3]. The local scheduler decides whether a generated task can be completed within its deadline in the node using the guarantee routine. If a new task is guaranteed for executing in the current node by the local scheduler, the task is enqueued in the task queue and executed in priority order by the dispatcher. Any task that was not guaranteed by the local scheduler is sent to the global scheduler.

The global scheduler uses a bidding scheme for loadsharing. When a task is sent by a local scheduler, the global scheduler sends a bid request to every other node and receives replies from available nodes. After receiving the replies, the global scheduler selects one proper node and sends the task to the selected node. If a node has received a bid request message from another node, the receiving node checks whether it can guarantee the bidden task. At that time, the global scheduler of the receiving node should consider the communication delay for sending the bid-reply message and migrating the task from the requesting node to the receiving node. The global scheduler sends a reply message when the node has enough surplus time to guarantee the bidden task. However, it is possible that the task migrated to the replying node cannot be guaranteed to be completed before its deadline since the node's surplus time can be changed after replying to the bid request [3]. In such a case, the bidding request will be done repeatedly until either there is a node that accepts the task or the least start time (deadline -execution time) of the task has already passed.

All messages to be sent to other nodes are enqueued in the output queue of the node for insertion into the interconnection network. These messages consist of reply and request messages for bidding and the tasks for migrating to other nodes. All incoming messages from other nodes are enqueued in the input queue and distributed by the packet handler. The packet handler sends the migrated tasks to the local scheduler to check whether the task can be executed on the node, and sends scheduling messages to the global scheduler for bidding. In a system which uses priority queues, all messages enqueued are processed in priority order. Otherwise, all messages are processed in FIFO order.

div.head: Simulation Assumption
div.p: The real-time parallel/distributed system considered in this paper consists of the functions described in Section 2.3. Such functions perform differently on various architectures due to the difference in many aspects such as the communication delay of the interconnection network and the number of processing nodes.

The simulator for real-time systems is built using the SimPack queuing library [SI. The delay of message transfer and task migration through the network is considered to be a constant. The priority queue or FIFO queue scheme can be selected for the task queue. Task preemption is not allowed in the simulation. The local scheduler uses non-preemptive least-laxity-first scheduling. Therefore, the priority of a task is defined as deadline laxity. For sharing loads among nodes and to use resources efficiently, the global scheduler uses a bidding scheme. The condition for a node to reply to a bid is given as a simulation parameter.

In the simulation, the distribution of inter-arrival time between tasks is assumed to be exponential. The distribution of execution time of tasks is also assumed to be exponential. A deadline is given as Q x e x e c u t i o n t i m e + @ where 01 is a given integer used to increase the deadline and @ is a randomly generated number between 1 to 300. In the simulation, we let Q be five, i.e., the deadline is 5 times larger than the execution time. The priority of a task is defined as the laxity of the deadline, i.e., priority = MAXINT -(deadlineezecution time).
We consider two types of systems in this paper. One is a regular system, whose node has no dedicated processing element for scheduling and packet handling.

The other is a system whose node has a dedicated processing element for scheduling and packet handling such as CODA [4, 51. We denote these systems as non-dedicated and dedicated, respectively. In the nondedicated system, scheduling overhead caused mainly by the guarantee routine is computed as a function of how many guaranteed tasks are currently on the node. We insert a stub process to the guaranteed task queue with the highest priority. The execution time of the stub process is computed by the above function. This is to reflect the scheduling overhead to the non-dedicated system. Hence, scheduling is done after completing the currently running task. On the other hand, the dedicated system does not require scheduling overhead since task scheduling does not disturb the currently guaranteed tasks. This fact is taken into account in the simulator.

The simulator is designed to measure the simulation results for the given specified period. This helps to get more reasonable simulation statistics, since we can ignore the initial unstable simulation results due to the system startup. All simulation results are measured between 1000 to 5000 unit time.

div.p: A system with dedicated processors for scheduling need not consider scheduling overhead during task scheduling. A system with normal processors, on which task execution and scheduling are performed, should consider scheduling overhead to complete the execution of guaranteed tasks before their deadlines. div.head: Queue Implementation
div.p: Table 2 shows the simulation results comparing the priority queue and the FIFO queue in the dedicated system for various communication delays. The mean task arrival time is fixed at 20. The FIFO queue and the priority queue have equal performance in a fast communication network. However, as the communication delay increases, the priority queue architecture outperforms the FIFO queue.

Next, we fixed the communication delay at 5 and tasks were generated to keep the node utilization similar. The simulation results are shown in Table 3. When the mean inter-arrival time and execution time are short, for example, (5,50), the priority queue system performs much better than the FIFO queue. The difference in GR between the two approaches is 0.125 which means that a system with priority queues guaranteed 12.5% more generated tasks than FIFO, but node utilization differs only by 3%. The difference comes from the migrated-guaranteed tasks. Since the tasks with small execution time most probably have small laxity, they are urgent tasks and the communication overhead is large compared with their laxity. A system with priority queues gives them high priority, and allows them to use the network quickly, but a system with FIFO queues cannot rescue them from being rejected. But these tasks do not greatly affect the processor utilization because they have small execution time. This implies that only a system with priority queues can guarantee urgent tasks with short execution time.

div.head: Number of Processing Nodes
div.p: In the system with priority queue, simulation was done for various numbers of nodes when the mean time of task arrival and execution time 2-tuple was fixed at (20,100), (10,100), and (10, 200). The results are shown in Table 4. If the demanded guarantee ratio GR is 0.99, which means that users require the system to guarantee more than 99% of tasks for the given environment, then 16 node is enough for a (20, 100) task-generating environment. Also, 32 and 64 nodes are required to get a GR of over 0.99 for (10, 100) and (10, 200) task generating environments, respectively.

div.head: Summary and Conclusion
div.p: We developed a real-time simulator for evaluating real-time system architectures. In this paper, we report on our simulations of various realtime performance-effecting design issues for two types of real-time architectures, both dedicated and nondedicated systems. We found that the dedicated system, which has no effect on task execution due to scheduling overhead, makes scheduling easy and enhances the confidence of in-time operation of guaranteed tasks. The simulation results can be summarized in three points. First, comparing FIFO and priority queue performance, priority-based communication and scheduling was proven to be more suitable for real-time systems than FIFO. Second, when a specific real-time architecture is given, it is possible to find the number of nodes sufficient to guarantee the user's real-time requirements (e.g., GR 2 0.99) for the given environments. Third, it is possible to find the optimal bid reply restriction if the network delay is predictable. Hence, designing a predictable network is one important aspect of designing real-time systems.

As an extension of this work, we are currently investigating the effect of system characteristics such as task preemption, priority policy, network topology, and routing/arbitration in predictable interconnection networks. Moreover, we are investigating the effect of task-executing environment factors such as network traffic and communication delay due to variation of message length. Also, an analysis of overall performance of real-time system architecture based on predictability of real-time systems is required for extensive comparison of real-time architectures.
